chunks: 1268 - And ʿAbdullāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Kāhilī heard him say:
Regarding the shortening in salat (prayer), a barīd in a barīd is twenty-four miles.

Then he said: My father, peace be upon him, used to say: The shortening was not prescribed on account of the swift mule or the fast riding beast; rather, it was prescribed according to the travel of the caravan.

Whenever a man's journey is eight farsakhs, then shortening is obligatory upon him. If his journey is four farsakhs and he intends to return the same day, then shortening is obligatory upon him. But if his journey is four farsakhs and he does not intend to return the same day, then he has the choice: if he wishes he may complete, and if he wishes he may shorten.

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرِ: shortening the four-unit salat (prayer) during travel
key_terms.الْقِطَارِ: the caravan, indicating normal travel pace
key_terms.بَرِيدٌ: a postal-distance measure used to determine travel length
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: farsakhs, a legal measure of travel distance
key_terms.مِيلًا: miles as a unit of distance

ai.seo_question: When does shortening salat (prayer) become obligatory during travel in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives the legal measure for qasr in salat (prayer) during travel and explains that the ruling is based on customary caravan travel, not unusually fast mounts. It also states that shortening is obligatory for a journey of eight farsakhs, and for four farsakhs when one intends to return the same day, while a four-farsakh journey without same-day return allows a choice.
